### Problem: Sum of All Odd Length Subarrays {#sec-cnt-p1-oddsum}

::: {.p-statement}
Given an array of positive integers `arr`, return the **sum of all possible odd-length subarrays** of `arr`. A subarray is a contiguous subsequence of the array.

For `arr = [1,4,2,5,3]` the answer is $58$: the odd-length windows are `[1]`, `[4]`, `[2]`, `[5]`, `[3]` (sums $1,4,2,5,3$), `[1,4,2]`, `[4,2,5]`, `[2,5,3]` (sums $7,11,10$) and `[1,4,2,5,3]` (sum $15$), and $1+4+2+5+3+7+11+10+15 = 58$.
Two more: `[1,2]` $\to$ $3$ (only the two single elements) and `[10,11,12]` $\to$ $66$.

Constraints: $1 \le n \le 100$, $1 \le arr[i] \le 1000$.

Source: [LC 1588 · Sum of All Odd Length Subarrays](https://leetcode.com/problems/sum-of-all-odd-length-subarrays/){.solved difficulty="Easy"}
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
The definition asks for a sum over a *set of windows*, and the first instinct is to build each window and add it up. Stop and re-read the sum: every term is an array element, and each element is added once **per window that covers it**. So you can hand the work over to the elements instead of the windows — that is the **contribution technique** of @sec-cnt-a1, and this problem is its cleanest possible illustration because the answer does not depend on the values at all, only on their positions.

How many windows cover slot $i$? A window is a choice of left end $a \le i$ and right end $b \ge i$, so there are $(i+1)$ choices for $a$, $(n-i)$ choices for $b$, and $(i+1)(n-i)$ windows in total that contain $i$. Of those, exactly the odd-length ones matter. A window has odd length $\iff$ $b-a$ is even $\iff$ $a$ and $b$ have the **same parity**, and counting the two parities on each side of $i$ gives exactly $\lceil (i+1)(n-i)/2 \rceil = ((i+1)(n-i)+1)//2$ odd-length windows — no case analysis on $n$ needed. Now each element is charged once: `answer = sum(arr[i] * ((i+1)*(n-i)+1) // 2)`, one pass, $O(n)$.

Read the table in the figure for `arr = [1,4,2,5,3]`: slot 2 (value $2$) sits in $9$ windows, $5$ of them odd-length, so it contributes $2 \times 5 = 10$. The five contributions $3,16,10,20,9$ add to $58$ — the same number the definition produces, but obtained with $n$ multiplications instead of $O(n^2)$ window sums.
:::

::: {.p-approach}
1. **Enumerate every odd window.** Loop over odd lengths and starts, and `sum()` the slice. $O(n^3)$ — the definition, written literally.
2. **Prefix sums, one subtraction per window.** Build `px` once (@sec-pref-def); a window sum is `px[i+L] - px[i]`, so the double loop becomes $O(n^2)$ with no inner re-scan.
3. **Charge each slot once (contest).** `((i+1)(n-i)+1)//2` is the number of odd-length windows covering $i$; multiply by the value and add. $O(n)$ time, $O(1)$ extra space, and the only rung that survives when $n$ becomes $10^5$.
:::

::: {#fig-cnt-p1-oddsum}

```{python}

#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    V.grid(ax, p, [["slot",          "0",  "1",  "2",  "3",  "4"],
                   ["value",         "1",  "4",  "2",  "5",  "3"],
                   ["windows covering it", "5", "8", "9", "8", "5"],
                   ["odd-length ones",  "3",  "4",  "5",  "4",  "3"],
                   ["contribution",  "3",  "16", "10", "20", "9"]],
           colors={(2, 3): "cyan", (3, 3): "amber", (4, 3): "green"}, cell_w=1.35)
V.show(draw)
```

Row 3 is $(i+1)(n-i)$, row 4 is $\lceil\cdot/2\rceil$, row 5 is value $\times$ row 4, and row 5 sums to $58$. Nothing in the table depends on the values, so the same shape works for any input of length $5$.

:::

::: {.panel-tabset .solution-forms}

#### Enumerate every odd window

::: {.form-next}
The statement as code: odd lengths outside, starts inside, `sum()` for the value of each window. $O(n^3)$ and unreadable at $n = 10^5$, but it is the reference every later rung is checked against.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("oddsum", "scan")
    assert str(final) == "58"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}

##### Python

```{python}
def odd_scan(arr):
    total = 0
    for length in range(1, len(arr) + 1, 2):          # 1, 3, 5, ...
        for i in range(len(arr) - length + 1):
            total += sum(arr[i:i + length])
    return total


assert odd_scan([1, 4, 2, 5, 3]) == 58
assert odd_scan([1, 2]) == 3
assert odd_scan([10, 11, 12]) == 66
assert odd_scan([7]) == 7                             # n = 1: one window
```

##### C++

```cpp
long long oddScan(vector<int>& a) {
    int n = a.size();
    long long total = 0;
    for (int len = 1; len <= n; len += 2)
        for (int i = 0; i + len <= n; ++i) {
            long long s = 0;
            for (int k = i; k < i + len; ++k) s += a[k];
            total += s;
        }
    return total;
}
```
:::

#### Prefix sums, one subtraction per window

::: {.form-next}
Same double loop, but the inner re-scan is gone: a prefix-sum array turns every window sum into one subtraction (@sec-pref-def), so $O(n^3)$ drops to $O(n^2)$. Still window-driven — the next rung changes *who* is being summed over.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("oddsum", "roll")
    assert str(final) == "58"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}

##### Python

```{python}
def odd_roll(arr):
    px = [0]
    for v in arr:
        px.append(px[-1] + v)
    total = 0
    for length in range(1, len(arr) + 1, 2):
        for i in range(len(arr) - length + 1):
            total += px[i + length] - px[i]           # sum of arr[i .. i+length-1]
    return total


assert odd_roll([1, 4, 2, 5, 3]) == 58
for _ in range(200):
    a = [random.randint(1, 1000) for _ in range(random.randint(1, 20))]
    assert odd_roll(a) == odd_scan(a)
```

##### C++

```cpp
long long oddRoll(vector<int>& a) {
    int n = a.size();
    vector<long long> px(n + 1);
    for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) px[i + 1] = px[i] + a[i];
    long long total = 0;
    for (int len = 1; len <= n; len += 2)
        for (int i = 0; i + len <= n; ++i)
            total += px[i + len] - px[i];
    return total;
}
```
:::

#### Charge each slot once (contest)

::: {.form-next}
Flip the summation: instead of walking windows and adding elements, walk elements and add their cover counts. One multiplication per slot, $O(n)$ total, and the code is three lines. This is the rung to memorise — everything else in @sec-cnt-p1 is the same swap with a harder cover count.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("oddsum", "contrib")
    assert str(final) == "58"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}

##### Python

```{python}
def odd_cover(arr):
    n = len(arr)
    return sum(v * (((i + 1) * (n - i) + 1) // 2) for i, v in enumerate(arr))


assert odd_cover([1, 4, 2, 5, 3]) == 58
assert odd_cover([1, 2]) == 3
assert odd_cover([10, 11, 12]) == 66
for _ in range(200):
    a = [random.randint(1, 1000) for _ in range(random.randint(1, 20))]
    assert odd_cover(a) == odd_scan(a)
# the ceiling only bites when both (i+1) and (n-i) are odd: for n = 5 the
# cover counts are [5,8,9,8,5] and the odd halves [3,4,5,4,3]
n = 5
assert [(i + 1) * (n - i) for i in range(n)] == [5, 8, 9, 8, 5]
assert [((i + 1) * (n - i) + 1) // 2 for i in range(n)] == [3, 4, 5, 4, 3]
assert 1 * 3 + 4 * 4 + 2 * 5 + 5 * 4 + 3 * 3 == 58
```

##### C++

```cpp
long long oddCover(vector<int>& a) {
    int n = a.size();
    long long total = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) {
        long long covers = (long long)(i + 1) * (n - i);
        total += (long long)a[i] * ((covers + 1) / 2);
    }
    return total;
}
```
:::

:::

::: {.p-complexity}
**Time** enumerate $O(n^3)$ (about $n^2/2$ windows, each re-summed); prefix sums $O(n^2)$; cover count $O(n)$. **Space** $O(n)$ for the prefix array, $O(1)$ for the cover rung.
**Size of the answer.** With $n \le 100$ and $arr[i] \le 1000$ the largest possible answer is $1000 \sum_i (i+1)(n-i) = 1000 \cdot 171700 = 1.7 \cdot 10^8$, which fits in a 32-bit `int`; the same formula at $n = 10^5$ overflows it by far, so the C++ tab accumulates in `long long` from the start.
:::

::: {.p-edge}
- $n = 1$: one window, answer `arr[0]`. The formula agrees: $((1)(1)+1)//2 = 1$.
- $n = 2$: no window of length $3$ exists, so only the two singles count ($3$ for `[1,2]`); the cover counts $[1, 1]$ come out of the same ceiling.
- Every value identical (say `[3,3,3]`): the cover counts are $[2,2,2]$, so the answer is $3(2+2+2) = 18$ — three singles of $3$ plus the whole array of $9$. Hand-check your formula against that number before trusting it.
- **Debug tip.** If your answer is roughly *double* the expected one, you counted all windows: $(i+1)(n-i)$ with no ceiling. On the sample that mistake gives $110$ instead of $58$ — a specific pair of numbers worth remembering when a reviewer asks what the failure looks like.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistakes"}
- **Using the array's length parity instead of the window's.** "Odd length" is a property of each window; the array length only decides how many odd lengths exist.
- **`(i+1)*(n-i+1)`** — the right end is $n-i$, not $n-i+1$: $b$ ranges over $i \ldots n-1$. Test on `[1,2]`, where the typo answers $6$ instead of $3$.
- **Floor instead of ceiling.** `covers // 2` drops the extra odd window whenever both factors are odd (slot 2 of a length-5 array: $9$ windows, $5$ odd). Use `(covers + 1) // 2`.
- **Re-summing inside the loop** on the prefix rung: `px[i+length] - px[i]` must not become `px[i+length] - px[i-1]`; index $-1$ silently reads the last prefix sum.
:::

**Variants.** @sec-cnt-p1-ranges keeps the summation swap but the quantity contributed by a slot is no longer "how many windows cover me" — it is "how many windows am I the maximum (or minimum) of", which needs a monotonic stack to answer. @sec-cnt-p3-ones counts windows with a property instead of their sums.

::: {.practice}
- [LC 1524 · Number of Sub-arrays With Odd Sum](https://leetcode.com/problems/number-of-sub-arrays-with-odd-sum/){difficulty="Medium"} — count the odd-sum windows instead of summing them; parity of prefix sums decides.
- [LC 907 · Sum of Subarray Minimums](https://leetcode.com/problems/sum-of-subarray-minimums/){difficulty="Medium"} — the same contribution swap with "am I the minimum" as the cover test.
- [LC 2395 · Find Subarrays With Equal Sum](https://leetcode.com/problems/find-subarrays-with-equal-sum/){difficulty="Easy"} — a fixed-length window sweep, to keep the window bookkeeping warm.
:::
